ai-at-work.title: ‘Odyssey’ director Christopher Nolan calls AI an obvious ‘Trojan horse’
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Christopher Nolan is warning that AI adoption in creative industries looks innocent on the surface but will fundamentally transform how work gets done once it's embedded in your systems. For digital workplace leaders, this matters because you're likely being pitched AI solutions that promise easy wins without anyone asking tough questions about long-term dependencies and skill atrophy. The irony is Nolan's right, but most organizations will wheel in the wooden horse anyway because quarterly earnings pressure beats strategic caution every single time.

ai-at-work.title: The agent evaluation gap: Enterprise AI organizations have a reality-alignment problem, not a coverage problem — and most are shipping to production anyway
ai-at-work.excerpt: Across 157 enterprises, organizations are granting AI agents more autonomy while trusting the evaluations meant to gate that autonomy less. Half have already shipped an agent that passed their interna
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Enterprise organizations are deploying AI agents to production despite knowing their evaluation methods don't reflect real-world performance, with half already shipping agents that failed after launch. This matters because digital workplace teams are inheriting these half-baked systems and getting blamed when the chatbot confidently gives terrible advice to actual users. Basically, companies are playing Russian roulette with automation while crossing their fingers and hoping IT can explain to frustrated employees why the AI they trusted just nuked a workflow.

ai-at-work.title: Agentic orchestration: Enterprise AI organizations have a deployment problem, not a platform problem — and most are calling chatbots agents
ai-at-work.excerpt: Across 101 enterprises, agent orchestration is consolidating onto model-provider platforms — Anthropic’s Claude leads by a wide margin — chosen for the gravity of the underlying model and judged on re
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Most enterprises are deploying what they call AI agents, but they're really just chatbots with extra steps, and they're building them on Claude because the underlying model is solid. This matters because digital workplace teams keep getting pitched agent solutions when what they actually need is a coherent deployment strategy that works across their messy, hybrid tech stacks. The honest truth is we're in the "slap agent paint on everything" phase of AI adoption, and it'll take another year before anyone figures out what orchestration actually looks like in production.

ai-at-work.title: Alibaba previews Qwen3.8, claims it’s second only to Claude Fable 5
ai-at-work.excerpt: Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. today previewed the most powerful artificial intelligence model in its Qwen family, Qwen3.8, and claimed the system trails only Anthropic PBC’s Claude Fable 5 among the worl
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Alibaba just dropped Qwen3.8, claiming it's the second most powerful AI model behind Claude Fable 5, and they're previewing it to the world at their Shanghai AI conference. For digital workplace folks, this matters because better AI models mean better search, smarter content discovery, and more capable copilots within your enterprise tools. That said, "second most powerful" claims are basically tech vendor karaoke at this point, and we'll believe the performance gap when our actual workplace productivity numbers improve.

tools-tech.title: OpenAI’s new hardware is a $230, 13-switch keyboard for Codex
tools-tech.excerpt: OpenAI is selling its first hardware — without any help from Jony Ive. It describes the Codex Micro as a “command center for agentic work” but it’s really a 13-switch wireless keyboard customized to h
tools-tech.dwp_take: OpenAI released a $230 wireless keyboard with 13 customizable switches designed specifically for monitoring AI agents running code. For digital workplace folks, this signals that AI agent management is becoming real enough that vendors think professionals will pay premium prices for specialized hardware to control it. Honestly, if people are dropping two hundred bucks on a keyboard just to babysit their AI before trust-fall season ends, we're definitely in the "still figuring this out" phase of agentic AI in the workplace.

industry-news.title: New FCC Proposal Pits Phone Privacy Against Fraud Prevention
industry-news.excerpt: The FCC has proposed requiring identity verification for phone activation, a move supporters say will fight fraud while critics warn it threatens privacy. The post New FCC Proposal Pits Phone Privacy
industry-news.dwp_take: The FCC wants to require identity verification when you activate a phone, claiming it will reduce fraud while privacy advocates cry foul. For digital workplace folks, this matters because it directly affects how your workforce gets mobile devices activated and authenticated, potentially adding friction to onboarding while raising questions about data security. Here's the thing: we've heard the "security versus privacy" argument a thousand times, and somehow we always end up collecting more data than necessary and protecting it worse than we promised.

industry-news.title: Apple Sued Over Hide My Email Privacy Claims
industry-news.excerpt: Apple faces a proposed class action alleging a Hide My Email flaw could expose users’ real addresses despite the company’s privacy claims. The post Apple Sued Over Hide My Email Privacy Claims appeare
industry-news.dwp_take: Apple's Hide My Email feature, which promises to mask users' real addresses, allegedly contains a flaw that exposes those addresses anyway, triggering a class action lawsuit. For digital workplace pros managing Apple device fleets and employee privacy, this is a reminder that privacy features only work if they actually work, and vendor promises need verification before rolling out company-wide. After three decades watching vendors claim security features that turn out to be theater, I'll believe Apple's privacy story when independent audits confirm it, not when their marketing says so.

industry-news.title: Cisco sounds alarm over new Russian malware campaign hitting firms in US and Europe
industry-news.excerpt: UAT-11795 is weaponizing legitimate software such as WebEx and Zoom to dupe victims
industry-news.dwp_take: Cisco discovered a Russian malware campaign that exploits legitimate tools like WebEx and Zoom to trick workers into downloading malicious software. This matters because your digital workplace infrastructure, the exact systems you've invested in for collaboration, just became an attack vector if your team isn't trained to spot the difference between real updates and fake ones. The irony is thick here: we spend billions making remote work seamless, then criminals weaponize that same seamlessness to slip past our defenses.

industry-news.title: Why Microsoft paused Patch Tuesday updates for some Dell devices
industry-news.excerpt: Select devices running Intel Innovation Platform Framework drivers encountered “poor performance”
industry-news.dwp_take: Microsoft hit the brakes on Patch Tuesday updates for certain Dell machines after Intel's Innovation Platform Framework drivers started tanking performance on those systems. This matters because it's a concrete reminder that even the biggest software vendors need to test their patches against real hardware configurations before shipping them out, and when they don't, it creates support nightmares for IT teams scrambling to manage inconsistent update schedules. Here's the thing: after three decades watching this play out, I've learned that "we'll patch it later" always costs more than getting it right the first time.
